extracted.intended_audience: Reviewers and Area Chairs for UAI 2024 (program committee members)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructions and evaluation criteria for reviewing papers submitted to the UAI 2024 conference (double-blind peer review). Covers reviewer/AC responsibilities, confidentiality, anonymity, conflicts, how to score papers on multiple axes, and required review content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibilities and workload
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers typically assess at most 6 papers. For each assigned paper, their main responsibilities consist of writing constructive and informative reviews, reading the author responses, participating in the discussions, and providing recommendations regarding acceptance or rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect deadlines and respond to emails promptly. You may revise your review as often as necessary by the reviewing deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area Chair responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Area Chairs typically oversee no more than 10 papers. For each assigned paper, their main responsibilities consist of finalizing the list of reviewers, facilitating the reviewing and discussion process, summarizing it in a meta-review, and providing a recommendation regarding paper acceptance or rejection to the program chairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May require close reading. ACs will also be asked to evaluate the quality of each review using three scores: 'exceeds expectations', 'meets expectations', and 'fails to meet expectations'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: By reviewing for UAI 2024, you agree to keep all material and information confidential (including but not limited to papers, meta-data, bidding data, messages and discussions related to reviewing, names of committee members involved, etc) and use them only for the purposes of reviewing your assigned manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use ideas/results from submissions for your own work until they are publicly available. Do not talk about or distribute submissions or reviewing content to anyone without prior approval from the program chairs, including other reviewers or area chairs. Delete all reviewing material (including code) at the end of the reviewing cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-blind reviewing and anonymization
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewing process is double blind at the level of reviewers and area chairs. Authors are responsible for anonymizing their submissions so that author identities and affiliations are not disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should use third person for their own work, omit names in acknowledgements, and avoid links revealing identity. If a submission is not adequately anonymized, inform the corresponding area chair. Do not attempt to discover author identities (e.g., by searching Google or arXiv); if you accidentally discover identities, do not disclose them and do not let them influence your decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors, Reviewers and Area Chairs will be asked to separately enter two types of conflicts into OpenReview: domain conflicts and individual conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declared conflicts are used to avoid assignments with conflicts. If you suspect you have a conflict with an assigned submission, contact the area chair or program chairs immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary material: what reviewers must read
rubrics_metrics.description: The main part of the submitted manuscript is at most 8 pages, and the manuscript may contain unlimited additional pages with references and appendices. Submission may also include supplementary material (source code or data) as a ZIP up to 50MB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your responsibility is to read and review the main part and to pay close attention to the additional appendices. Looking at further supplementary material (e.g., provided source code ZIP) is at your discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executing code and clicking links (safety guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no guarantees about submitted code and links; they may contain vulnerabilities or reveal your IP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you run supplementary source code, do so in a secure environment (Docker container, VM, or network-isolated cloud instance). Be aware links may log visitor IPs and reveal identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting instructions compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions must follow the UAI LaTeX template and formatting instructions. Papers must be submitted as PDF files. The main part of the manuscript is limited to at most 8 pages including all figures and tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplementary text should be included after the main paper (after references, starting on a new page) in the same PDF. Authors must not change the template. If you are assigned a paper that is overlength or appears to violate the proceedings format (e.g., decreased margins or font size), notify the area chair immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual submissions prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers currently under review or accepted/published in a refereed venue with proceedings may not be submitted to UAI. This also applies to substantially identical works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting the same/substantially similar work to another refereed venue with proceedings while it is under review at UAI is disallowed. Conferences/workshops without proceedings, technical report repositories and arXiv are NOT considered dual submissions. If you suspect a dual submission, contact the area chair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author response (rebuttal) handling
rubrics_metrics.description: After the initial review period, authors may submit responses to their reviews to correct misunderstandings, point out missed aspects, or disagree with parts of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read each rebuttal carefully and with an open mind. Consider whether authors' comments change your opinion about the paper or indicate you overlooked something.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion period participation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a discussion period (two stages) during which reviewers, authors (stage 1), and ACs discuss the paper. Discussions are led by the area chairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read other reviews and the authors’ response at the start of discussion. Engage professionally and politely, keep an open mind, and participate actively—especially on borderline papers and when assessments vary widely. You may change your opinion but should not give in to undue influence; full consensus is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review content: Q1 Summary and contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Q1: Summarize the paper’s motivation and key contributions in a few lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section may not provide much new information to authors but is valuable to area chairs and program chairs. (Max. 500 characters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Review content: Q2 Assessment axes (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Q2: Assess the work along the following axes: originality/novelty, soundness/technical quality, whether claims are supported by convincing evidence, clarity of writing, reproducibility, ethical aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More detailed information for each axis is provided in separate sub-criteria (see corresponding metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / novelty (Q2 axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: How novel are the concepts, problems addressed, methods introduced, or insights obtained in the paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 4: Excellent — main ideas ground-breaking. 3: Good — non-trivial advances over state-of-the-art. 2: Fair — contributes some new ideas. 1: Poor — not novel or incremental progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness / technical quality (Q2 axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper technically sound?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 4: Excellent — confident paper is technically sound, carefully checked. 3: Good — appears sound, not carefully checked. 2: Fair — minor, easily fixable technical flaws not impacting main results. 1: Poor — major technical flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent to which claims are supported by evidence (Q2 axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the paper's claims supported by convincing evidence (experiments, proofs, code, references, assumptions)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 4: Excellent — all claims supported by very convincing evidence (comprehensive eval, rigorous proofs, detailed code, precise refs, realistic assumptions). 3: Good — main claims supported by convincing evidence. 2: Fair — somewhat supported but evaluation weak/missing baselines/insufficient rigor. 1: Poor — authors fail to convincingly back main claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility (Q2 axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results (theorems, experimental results) in the paper easily reproducible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 4: Excellent — key resources (proofs, code, data) available and details comprehensively described. 3: Good — resources available and details sufficiently described. 2: Fair — resources unavailable but details sufficiently described for an expert. 1: Poor — key details or resources incomplete/unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of writing (Q2 axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper well-organized and clearly written?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 4: Excellent — well-organized and clearly written. 3: Good — well organized but presentation could improve. 2: Fair — somewhat clear but important details missing/unclear. 1: Poor — unclear and very hard to understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q3: Main strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the main strengths of the work, considering the same axes as in Q2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention as many main strengths as there are; avoid minor points here. Be specific. (Max. 3000 characters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Q4: Main weaknesses and tone guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the main weaknesses of the work, considering the same axes as in Q2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your comments should be detailed, specific, and polite. Avoid vague, subjective complaints. Provide citations for claims such as 'incremental' and suggest improvements (e.g., datasets, metrics, sensitivity analyses). Avoid being dismissive or using inappropriate language. (Max. 3000 characters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Q5: Detailed comments to the authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide constructive criticism and feedback to help improve the work or its presentation (presentation suggestions, missing refs, minor mistakes, typos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include questions for authors and be explicit if you want specific clarifications during the author response (e.g., 'I would like to see results of experiment X'). Focus on points important for the decision because the rebuttal length is limited. (Max. 200000 characters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Q6: Overall score and category definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an overall evaluation of the paper, weighing reasons to accept and reject. Use integer categories 1–10 with descriptive definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score definitions: 10 Award quality (technically flawless, highly original, exceptionally strong evidence, excellent reproducibility, no ethical issues, large impact potential); 9 Very Strong Accept; 8 Strong Accept; 7 Accept; 6 Weak Accept; 5 Borderline accept; 4 Borderline reject; 3 Reject; 2 Strong Reject; 1 Very Strong Reject. Guidance on distributions: ideally <=25% in Accept+Strong Accept+Very Strong+Award, <=20% in Strong Accept+Very Strong+Award, <=10% in Very Strong+Award, <=1% Award Quality. Use full range where appropriate and do not calibrate to expected acceptance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q7: Justification for overall score
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain in a few lines how you arrived at your overall assessment and which aspects you weighed most heavily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise explanation, focusing on the trade-offs between strengths and weaknesses. (Max. 500 characters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Q8: Confidence in your score
rubrics_metrics.description: Rate your confidence in your assessment on a 1–5 scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5 Very confident — checked all points carefully and are an expert. 4 Quite confident — tried to check important points and are familiar with the topic. 3 Somewhat confident — may have missed some aspects. 2 Not very confident — likely missed or did not understand some key details. 1 Not confident — evaluation is an educated guess or outside your area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q9: Compliance certification
rubrics_metrics.description: I have read the UAI reviewing instructions and certify that I comply with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically certify confidentiality and deleting reviewing material at the end of the review cycle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Q10: Ethical concerns flagging
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the submission raise potential ethical concerns (methods, applications, or data that can create/reinforce unfair bias or have primary purpose of harm)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer yes/no and provide a brief explanation if yes. This flag is optional and independent of the overall rating; your duty is to only flag papers needing further ethical evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area Chair evaluation of review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Area Chairs will evaluate the quality of each review using three categorical scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three scores: 'exceeds expectations', 'meets expectations', and 'fails to meet expectations' — used to identify top reviewers and for honourable mention.
